newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major offers key concession to Euro rebels.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major offers key concession to Euro rebels.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Thursday offered a key concession to rebels in his party opposed to a European single currency in a bid to end divisions and get a grip on his campaign for the May 1 election.

Major told an impromptu news conference in north-west England that allowing members of parliament a free vote on whether or not to join a single European currency was "almost certainly the right way to handle it".
His announcement took everyone by surprise -- including Major's own finance minister, Kenneth Clarke.

The move was nevertheless hailed by aides and so-called Eurosceptics opposed to European integration as a dramatic but workable solution to a problem that has dogged Major's every effort to unite his party for his six years in office.
Opposition parties leapt on the news as a desperate move by a leader lagging in the polls and doomed to defeat.
Labour's economics spokesman Gordon Brown told reporters: "We now have a leader who has lost control of his party."

Menzies Campbell of the minority Liberal Democrats, said: "This morning...the prime minister was not only abdicating the leadership of the warring Tory (Conservative) party but completely capitulating to the Tory Euro-rebels."

The shift over Europe came as Major fought to heal festering divisions in his ruling party over Europe: the same issue that led to his predecessor Margaret Thatcher being ousted as party leader and prime minister seven years ago.

Major has been left reeling by the decision of two junior ministers and more than 200 Conservative candidates to campaign against a single currency in defiance of government policy, which is to wait and see if it is in Britain's interest to join.
Major said it was "frustrating" that some members of his party were "unwisely" stepping out of line.

But he repeated his appeal, made first in a personal television broadcast on Wednesday night and backed up in full-page newspaper adverts on Thursdays, for people not to tie his hands ahead of negotiations on Europe's future.
Major told reporters on his plane as he carried on a relentless schedule of campaigning for re-election that he was delighted Europe was at the top of the election agenda.
But he admitted that he had little choice but to accept a free vote as it would be hard to force MPs to vote for a single currency if they opposed the project.
Some of the shine was taken off the news by the admission in a radio interview by Clarke, the Chancellor of the Exchequer, that he did not know about the announcement in advance.
Asked if he had been consulted, Clarke said: "No, I wasn't", before hastily backing Major's line.

Labour's Brown immediately weighed in, accusing Major of making up policy as he went along. He told a radio interviewer: "It is an astonishing admission by the Chancellor that on a vital economic decision he was not even consulted."
Major's aides believe the move will help lift the campaign.
But polls give little comfort so far to Major, whose party has now been in office for 18 years.

An opinion poll in Thursday's Times showed a clear majority backed Major's policy of taking part in negotiations on the European single currency, only deciding at the end whether taking part was in Britain's interests.
But this did not translate into votes.
Support for the Conservatives slipped two points to 32 percent in the last week, putting Labour 17 points ahead -- enough for a majority of well over 80 seats in parliament.
